blocks.content: 1. What Happens When You Type a URL and Hit Enter
blocks.text: 1. What Happens When You Type a URL and Hit Enter

blocks.content: This is very often the opening question of an entire networking interview, precisely because a strong answer requires connecting ideas across several different modules of this course at once. DNS resolution happens first, translating the domain name to an IP address. A TCP handshake establishes connectivity, followed by a TLS handshake if the connection is HTTPS. Only then does the actual HTTP request and response exchange happen, followed finally by the browser rendering the result, exactly the full journey traced in the journey-of-a-request topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019259725-666208001.png
blocks.alt: A strong answer traces the full journey: DNS, TCP, optionally TLS, the HTTP exchange itself, and finally rendering

blocks.content: 2. TCP Versus UDP, and When to Actually Use Each
blocks.text: 2. TCP Versus UDP, and When to Actually Use Each

blocks.content: Be ready to state this precisely, not just name both protocols. TCP trades speed for guaranteed, reliable, ordered delivery, the right choice whenever correctness genuinely matters more than raw speed. UDP trades that guarantee for genuine speed and minimal overhead, the right choice when a late or missing piece of data is actually less harmful than the delay of waiting for it to be resent.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019261392-707212944.png
blocks.alt: TCP fits reliability critical data; UDP fits speed critical data where a late or lost piece matters less than delay

blocks.content: 3. Why the Handshake and the Close Have Different Step Counts
blocks.text: 3. Why the Handshake and the Close Have Different Step Counts

blocks.content: A genuinely common, more probing follow up. Opening a TCP connection only needs one shared agreement between both sides, achievable in three steps. Closing needs each of the two genuinely independent directions of the connection to be closed on its own, requiring four steps. Being able to explain the WHY here, not just recite the step counts, is what separates a strong answer.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019263020-677393281.png
blocks.alt: Opening needs one shared agreement, three steps; closing needs two independent directions to each close, four steps

4. Forward Proxy Versus Reverse Proxy

A classic, commonly confused pair. A forward proxy sits in front of clients, representing them to the wider internet. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers, representing and protecting them from the outside world. Remembering which side of the connection each one actually sits on is the entire key to keeping them straight under interview pressure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019264665-110454204.png
blocks.alt: A forward proxy represents clients reaching outward; a reverse proxy represents and protects servers from the outside

blocks.content: 5. How a CDN Actually Makes Things Faster
blocks.text: 5. How a CDN Actually Makes Things Faster

blocks.content: Be ready to explain the actual mechanism, not just that a CDN exists. A CDN spreads copies of content across geographically distributed edge servers, letting a user request be served from a genuinely nearby location instead of one distant origin, directly reducing the physical distance component of latency.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019266218-461956832.png
blocks.alt: A CDN reduces latency specifically by serving content from a nearby edge server instead of one distant origin

blocks.content: 6. A Deliberately Tricky Follow Up

Why might a website with plenty of available bandwidth still feel genuinely slow to use. This tests whether the latency versus bandwidth distinction genuinely sank in. The answer, latency, not bandwidth, is very often the actual bottleneck, a connection can move plenty of data per second while individual pieces of data still take a real, long time to arrive due to distance, hops, or congestion.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019267903-442967189.png
blocks.alt: A slow feeling site despite plenty of bandwidth is very often a latency problem, not a bandwidth one, a classic distinguishing question

blocks.title: A great follow up to have ready yourself
blocks.content: If asked this, a genuinely strong answer also mentions concrete fixes, a CDN for distance related latency, or investigating actual network bottlenecks, tying the answer directly back to real, practical solutions covered elsewhere in this course.
7. How to Actually Prepare With This Topic
blocks.text: 7. How to Actually Prepare With This Topic

blocks.content: The strongest networking interview answers consistently explain WHY a mechanism exists and what specific problem it actually solves, not just its name or definition. Explaining why TCP needs a handshake at all, not just that it has one, is what genuinely distinguishes a strong, confident answer from a shallow, memorized one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784019269421-444183524.png
blocks.alt: A weak answer just names a term correctly; a strong answer explains why that mechanism exists and what problem it solves

blocks.title: One habit that reliably improves any networking answer
blocks.content: Before answering, silently ask yourself, am I explaining WHAT this is, or WHY it exists and what it actually solves. The second kind of answer is consistently the one that stands out in a real interview.
